questions.q: Hasan Basri said the world meant less to the Companions than the dust under their feet. Why, according to the article, did they live so simply?
options: Because they could afford nothing better
Not quite. The article says: By choice – to keep free of the distractions of wealth and stay focused on the Hereafter.
Because they were ordered to by rulers
Not quite. The article says: By choice – to keep free of the distractions of wealth and stay focused on the Hereafter.
Because fine clothes were unknown then
Not quite. The article says: By choice – to keep free of the distractions of wealth and stay focused on the Hereafter.
By choice – to keep free of the distractions of wealth and stay focused on the Hereafter
Yes. “Be in this world as if you were a stranger or a traveller.”
questions.rationale: “They wore simple garments… and lived frugally, not out of necessity but out of choice, to avoid the distractions of material wealth.”

questions.q: According to the saying of the Prophet discussed in the article, on what does the reward of worship depend?
options: How many people witness it
Not quite. The article says: The depth of consciousness with which it is performed, not its quantity or outward form.
The depth of consciousness with which it is performed, not its quantity or outward form
Right. The heart “quivers with the remembrance of God.”
The number of acts performed
Not quite. The article says: The depth of consciousness with which it is performed, not its quantity or outward form.
The length of each act
Not quite. The article says: The depth of consciousness with which it is performed, not its quantity or outward form.
questions.rationale: “The reward for these acts is not contingent on their quantity or outward form; rather, it hinges on the depth of consciousness with which they are performed.”

questions.q: Is conscious worship limited to formal rituals, in the article’s view?
options: No – everyday acts such as honesty, kindness and doing one’s duty become worship when done to seek God’s pleasure
Yes. Awareness is carried into daily life.
No – but only acts done in public count
Not quite. The article says: No – everyday acts such as honesty, kindness and doing one’s duty become worship when done to seek God’s pleasure.
Yes – only prayer and fasting count
Not quite. The article says: No – everyday acts such as honesty, kindness and doing one’s duty become worship when done to seek God’s pleasure.
Yes – it requires a place of worship
Not quite. The article says: No – everyday acts such as honesty, kindness and doing one’s duty become worship when done to seek God’s pleasure.
questions.rationale: “Everyday actions, when performed with the intention of seeking God’s pleasure, can become acts of worship. This includes kindness, honesty, and fulfilling one’s duties.”

questions.article: Shift the Focus to Duty-Based Approach
questions.q: The article compares citizens to bricks. What is the point of the comparison?
options: A nation built of people of tempered, dependable character stands firm, like a building of kiln-fired bricks
Well read. Otherwise it is a sandcastle.
Old bricks are better than new
Not quite. The article says: A nation built of people of tempered, dependable character stands firm, like a building of kiln-fired bricks.
Citizens should all be alike
Not quite. The article says: A nation built of people of tempered, dependable character stands firm, like a building of kiln-fired bricks.
A nation needs more buildings
Not quite. The article says: A nation built of people of tempered, dependable character stands firm, like a building of kiln-fired bricks.
questions.rationale: “Citizens with a character so tempered that they can be depended upon through thick and thin—like the kiln-fired bricks—build a nation in the long run.”

questions.article: Shift the Focus to Duty-Based Approach
questions.q: What does the article say happens when people carry out their duties?
options: They lose their rights
Not quite. The article says: They receive their rights as a natural result – “It is in giving that we receive”.
Nothing changes
Not quite. The article says: They receive their rights as a natural result – “It is in giving that we receive”.
They receive their rights as a natural result – “It is in giving that we receive”
Correct. Rights cannot be won by demands alone.
They must still demand their rights loudly
Not quite. The article says: They receive their rights as a natural result – “It is in giving that we receive”.
questions.rationale: “When people carry out their duties, they will automatically receive their rights… they should shift the focus of their efforts from the rights-based approach to the duty-based approach.”

questions.article: The Believer Must Also Be a Traveller
questions.q: What is tawassum, as the article explains it?
options: Travelling as far as possible
Not quite. The article says: Drawing spiritual lessons from ordinary material experiences through reflection.
Avoiding worldly experience
Not quite. The article says: Drawing spiritual lessons from ordinary material experiences through reflection.
Drawing spiritual lessons from ordinary material experiences through reflection
Yes. Travel plus tawassum leads to realization of God.
Keeping a record of journeys
Not quite. The article says: Drawing spiritual lessons from ordinary material experiences through reflection.
questions.rationale: “Tawassum is a Quranic term that signifies the elicitation of spiritual lessons from material phenomena.”

questions.article: The Believer Must Also Be a Traveller
questions.q: What reflection does the article draw from a return ticket?
options: One should always plan to come home early
Not quite. The article says: Death is the one journey with no return ticket – a reminder of the Hereafter.
Travel is expensive
Not quite. The article says: Death is the one journey with no return ticket – a reminder of the Hereafter.
Death is the one journey with no return ticket – a reminder of the Hereafter
Right. An everyday object becomes a lesson.
Tickets should be bought in advance
Not quite. The article says: Death is the one journey with no return ticket – a reminder of the Hereafter.
questions.rationale: “Death is the ultimate journey with no return ticket, leading to the Hereafter.”

questions.q: How does the article reconcile “creation in six days” with the scientific view of a very long process?
options: By holding that the verses are not meant to be understood
Not quite. The article says: The Arabic word for “day” can mean a period of time, so the six days are six long stages.
By taking each day as exactly 24 hours
Not quite. The article says: The Arabic word for “day” can mean a period of time, so the six days are six long stages.
The Arabic word for “day” can mean a period of time, so the six days are six long stages
Yes. Verses speak of a day like a thousand, or fifty thousand, years.
By setting aside the scientific view
Not quite. The article says: The Arabic word for “day” can mean a period of time, so the six days are six long stages.
questions.rationale: “The word can also have the broader meaning of a ‘period of time’… we may interpret the creation of the heavens and the earth to have taken place in six ‘periods of time’.”

questions.q: A young officer fell to his death moments after standing triumphant on a summit. What does the article say his story is?
options: Proof that ambition is wrong
Not quite. The article says: The story of every one of us – death may come at the very height of success, so one should prepare for what follows.
A warning against mountaineering
Not quite. The article says: The story of every one of us – death may come at the very height of success, so one should prepare for what follows.
The story of every one of us – death may come at the very height of success, so one should prepare for what follows
Exactly. “Every human being is bound to taste death.”
An unusual accident with no wider meaning
Not quite. The article says: The story of every one of us – death may come at the very height of success, so one should prepare for what follows.
questions.rationale: “The story of Lieutenant Lamba is not the story of just one individual. It is the story of every one of us.”

questions.q: What does the answer on parenting call the greatest gift a father can give his children?
options: A comfortable home
Not quite. The article says: Education and good manners, not material things.
Education and good manners, not material things
Well read. Daughters and sons alike.
Freedom from all work
Not quite. The article says: Education and good manners, not material things.
A large inheritance
Not quite. The article says: Education and good manners, not material things.
questions.rationale: “The greatest gift a father can give his children is education and good manners, not material things.”
